displayQuote: Hell, there are no rules here. We're trying to accomplish something

meta.title: Who really said "Hell, there are no rules here. We're trying to accomplish something"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edison probably did say it — but not like that. The line comes from chemist M. A. Rosanoff's 1932 Harper's memoir; the polished wording dates to 1996.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hell, there are no rules here. We're trying to accomplish something'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Edison, but the 1932 source reads "Hell! there ain't no rules around here!" One witness, published after Edison died. Here's the evidence.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credibly credited to Edison, but there is no primary source in his own hand and the smooth sentence people quote is not the documented wording. The whole story rests on one witness: the chemist M. A. Rosanoff, who published it in Harper’s Magazine in September 1932 — after Edison’s death — recalling an exchange at the West Orange laboratory around 1903, where he prints the reply in dialect as “Hell! there ain’t no rules around here! We are tryin’ to accomplish somep’n!”

source.excerpt:
“Mr. Edison, please tell me what laboratory rules you want me to observe.”
“Hell! there ain’t no rules around here! We are tryin’ to accomplish somep’n!”
trail: The earliest source located by Quote Investigator ↗ is M. A. Rosanoff’s article “Edison in His Laboratory” in Harper’s Magazine, September 1932 (vol. 165, pp. 402–403), describing an incident from around 1903. QI prints the words as “Hell! there ain’t no rules around here! We are tryin’ to accomplish somep’n!”

Wikiquote ↗ carries the same dialect wording in its 1900s section, citing Harper’s Monthly, September 1932, and supplies the scene: Rosanoff joined the West Orange, New Jersey team in 1903 and asked which laboratory rules he should observe.

Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ then follows the line through a 1947 New York Times piece by Waldemar Kaempffert, a December 1959 Popular Science retelling that keeps the dialect, and an Executive Speeches item of October–November 1996 in which the phrasing is regularized to the familiar modern sentence.

The witness was real: Martin André Rosanoff ↗ (1874–1951) was a Russian-American chemist known for the Fischer–Rosanoff convention — though his Wikipedia biography makes no mention of Edison, and no Edison-side record of the exchange has surfaced.
source.excerptNote: The question is how Rosanoff recalled putting it on joining the West Orange staff, as summarised on Wikiquote ↗; the reply is the wording Quote Investigator ↗ gives from the September 1932 Harper’s text. The sentence people quote today — “Hell, there are no rules here. We’re trying to accomplish something” — is a later regularization of it.

source.rightsHolder: Harper’s Magazine (published in 1932 by Harper & Brothers) and the estate of M. A. Rosanoff
source.rightsNote: The only documented text of this remark sits inside a magazine article first published in September 1932, which falls on the in-copyright side of the pre-1931 line this site uses; its precise US status would turn on whether the 1932 issue’s copyright was renewed, which we have not verified, so we treat it conservatively as protected. The familiar modern wording is later still — Quote Investigator traces it to a 1996 publication. Edison’s spoken words are not themselves a published work, but every version in circulation descends from copyrighted print, so we quote only the short passage needed to document the attribution.

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.kicker: The man it is credited to
author.heading: Thomas Edison
author.bio: Thomas Edison (1847–1931) was an American inventor and businessman whose phonograph, motion-picture and electric-light work made him the most famous technologist of his age. In 1887 he began a far larger laboratory complex at West Orange, New Jersey — a facility the Rutgers Edison Papers project describes as unsurpassed until the twentieth century, combining workshops, library and manufacturing on one site. It is that lab, not the earlier Menlo Park one, that the “no rules” story is set in.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets misquoted here
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from another author — every version Quote Investigator found credits Edison. What goes wrong is the wording, the place, and the confidence with which it is presented as documented fact.

items.why: “Hell, there are no rules here. We’re trying to accomplish something” is not what the 1932 article prints. Quote Investigator ↗ gives the Harper’s text as “Hell! there ain’t no rules around here! We are tryin’ to accomplish somep’n!” and traces the regularized phrasing to an Executive Speeches item of October–November 1996.

The line is routinely staged at Menlo Park — that is how the reader who wrote in to Quote Investigator ↗ had encountered it, and QI’s investigation does not support that setting. Wikiquote ↗ places the exchange at West Orange, New Jersey in 1903, and Rutgers dates the founding of the West Orange laboratory ↗ to 1887 — so a 1903 conversation was not a Menlo Park one.

It is presented as settled, but it is one man’s recollection. Quote Investigator ↗ states that the correctness of the quotation rests on the accuracy of M. A. Rosanoff’s memory, and adds only that if the incident occurred it was probably quite memorable for him.

items.who: Quoted as if Edison confirmed it
items.why: Edison died on 18 October 1931 (Wikipedia ↗) and the account appeared in Harper’s Magazine in September 1932 (Quote Investigator ↗). He was never in a position to confirm or deny it.

misattribution.truthLine: The remark is genuinely Edison’s so far as anyone can show — but it survives only through the chemist M. A. Rosanoff, in Harper’s Magazine, September 1932, in dialect, about an exchange around 1903. The tidy sentence quoted today is a twentieth-century paraphrase of that one account, traced by Quote Investigator ↗ to 1996.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Edison’s West Orange complex, begun in 1887, was one of the first places where invention was organised as an industry rather than practised as a craft — machine shops, a chemical lab, a library and manufacturing on a single site. A newly hired chemist asking which rules applied was asking a perfectly sensible question of a workplace that looked, from the outside, like a factory.

The reply became famous because it inverts the expectation: the most systematic inventor in America is made to say that system is beside the point. That is why the line has had a long second life in management writing and startup culture — and also why it kept getting tidied up. A boss barking in dialect and spitting on the floor is an anecdote; a crisp epigram is a slide.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology runs: the 1932 Harper’s account in dialect; a partial version in a 1947 New York Times piece by Waldemar Kaempffert; a 1959 Popular Science retelling that keeps the dialect spellings; and a 1996 Executive Speeches item in which the phrasing is regularized to the version circulating today.

Each step removes texture and adds polish. Nothing in that chain is a new piece of evidence about what Edison said — it is the same single 1932 recollection being restated, so the modern wording is best read as a paraphrase of Rosanoff, not as a second source.
context.pull: The most systematic inventor in America, quoted as saying that systems are beside the point.
